title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description: Brute force to optimized: rechecking every window from scratch versus a single coordinated sliding window tracking the most frequent character's count.

blocks.text: Given a string s consisting of only uppercase English letters, and an integer k, you may replace at most k characters of s with any other uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest substring containing a single repeated letter that can be achieved this way.

blocks.caption: Grow the window; shrink it only when the replacements needed exceed the budget k

blocks.text: Given a string s of uppercase letters and an integer k, find the length of the longest substring that can be turned into all one repeated letter using at most k character replacements.

blocks.title: Analogy: Repainting a Group's Jerseys to Match
blocks.text: Like looking at a lineup of teammates wearing a mix of jersey colors and figuring out the largest consecutive group you could repaint into a single solid color, using only a limited number of repaints.

blocks.caption: Repaint the minority jerseys within a group, using a limited repaint budget, to find the largest solid-color group

blocks.text: Edge case: k equals the length of s
When k is large enough to replace every character, the entire string can always be made into one repeated letter, so the answer is simply the full length of s.
Before trying every substring and counting replacements from scratch, notice that a window's replacement cost depends only on its single most frequent character.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Within any window, the cheapest way to make every character the same is to keep the MOST FREQUENT character as-is and replace every other character in the window.

Observation 2: This means the number of replacements a window needs is exactly (window length) minus (the count of its most frequent character).

Observation 3: Grow a window from the right, tracking a running count of each letter seen and the highest single count among them. Whenever the window's required replacements exceed k, shrink from the left.

Observation 4: A subtle but important detail: the tracked "highest count so far" never needs to decrease, even after shrinking, since a window can only ever grow to be at least as long as the best one already found; this simplifies the bookkeeping without affecting correctness.

Whenever a problem asks for the longest window where "changing up to k elements to match the majority" is a valid strategy, tracking the count of the single most frequent element, alongside a variable-size sliding window, solves it in one pass.
This "track the most frequent element, and treat everything else as the cost to fix" idea is the core trick that makes this problem tractable in linear time.
For every possible starting position, extend the window one character at a time, checking after each extension whether the required replacements still fit within the budget k.

items: For every possible starting position, extend the window one character at a time, maintaining a count of each letter seen so far in this window.
At each extension, compute the window length minus its most frequent character's count; if this fits within k, update the best length found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh count map is built for each starting position, since each independent window's letter counts need to be tracked separately.
max_count is updated every time a character is added, always reflecting the single most frequent letter seen so far in the current window.
The check (length minus max_count at most k) directly encodes "the number of characters that would need replacing fits within budget".

blocks.text: Every window's true replacement cost is computed directly, so the correct longest valid substring is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, since each of the n starting positions can extend up to n characters.
Space: O(1) extra, since only 26 possible letters are ever tracked.

Limitation: restarting the character counts from scratch at every new starting position ignores that a single coordinated sliding window, growing and shrinking together, can answer the same question in one linear pass.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force treats every starting position independently, discarding useful information between them. Instead, grow a single window from the right, tracking both a running letter-frequency count and the highest single count seen (the most frequent letter in the current window). Whenever the window's implied replacement cost (window length minus that highest count) exceeds k, shrink from the left by one position. Since the window only ever grows overall (it never needs to shrink below its previous best length), the entire process runs in a single linear pass.

Maintain a window with a left and right boundary, along with a frequency count of letters in the window and the highest such count seen. Grow the window by advancing right. Whenever (window length minus the highest frequency count) exceeds k, shrink from the left by one position. Track the maximum window length seen throughout.
Grow the window from the right, tracking the most frequent character's count, and shrink from the left only when the replacement budget is exceeded.

codes.python:
def character_replacement(s, k):
    count = [0] * 26
    left = 0
    max_count = 0
    best = 0
    for right in range(len(s)):
        idx = ord(s[right]) - ord('A')
        count[idx] += 1
        max_count = max(max_count, count[idx])                             # the most frequent character seen in the window so far
        while (right - left + 1) - max_count > k:                            # too many replacements would be needed, shrink
            count[ord(s[left]) - ord('A')] -= 1
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(character_replacement("AABABBA", 1))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since left and right each advance forward at most n times total across the whole pass.
Space: O(1) extra, since only 26 possible letters are ever tracked.

A window's cheapest path to becoming uniform is always to keep its most frequent letter and replace everything else, so (window length minus most-frequent-count) is exactly the true minimum number of replacements that window needs. Once this exceeds k, shrinking from the left removes exactly one character, and repeating the check ensures the window only ever holds a state where the replacement cost is within budget, or is in the process of being corrected back into budget.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Window's replacement cost is within budget k","Keep growing the window by advancing right"],["Window's replacement cost exceeds budget k","Shrink the window from the left by exactly one position"]]}

items: The frequency count is updated every time a character enters the window (on growth) or leaves it (on shrink), always reflecting the window's current contents.

max_count is intentionally never decreased when the window shrinks; this looks like it might introduce a subtle bug, but since the algorithm only cares about the LONGEST valid window ever found, an outdated (too-high) max_count only ever prevents an unnecessary shrink, never an incorrect answer, since best is only updated using the current, correctly-sized window at each step.
The while loop shrinks the window by exactly one position whenever the current implied cost exceeds k, keeping the window's cost within budget on the way back down.

blocks.text: The key insight, tracking the count of the single most frequent character in a window as a proxy for its replacement cost, is what turns this problem into a standard variable-size sliding window, the same shape used across many string and array problems.

items: Recomputing the most frequent character's count from scratch on every shrink, instead of maintaining it incrementally (and understanding why an outdated, too-high value is harmless here).
Confusing "the window's length minus its most frequent count" with some other unrelated cost formula.
Shrinking the window more than one position at a time inside the while loop, when a single position at a time is both correct and sufficient here.

items: Explicitly state the "keep the majority letter, replace the rest" insight out loud, since recognizing this reframes the entire problem into a simple count comparison.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the longest substring where up to k characters can be changed to make it uniform" points toward tracking the count of the single most frequent character within a variable-size sliding window.

items: How would this change if replacements had different costs depending on which letter was being changed to which? The simple "length minus most-frequent-count" formula would no longer directly apply, and a more general weighted approach would be needed.
What if you needed to return the actual substring, not just its length? Track the best window's starting index and length together, updating both whenever a new best length is found.

How would you solve this if only two specific characters could ever be interchanged (a more limited case)? A similar sliding window, tracking counts of just those two characters, would apply directly.
Shares its variable-size sliding window shape with Minimum Size Subarray Sum, though the growth/shrink CONDITION differs (a replacement-budget check here, versus a sum threshold there).

The same "track the count of the most frequent/least frequent element as a proxy for a cost" idea reappears in Max Consecutive Ones III, a very similar problem where the "replacement" is specifically 0s becoming 1s.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (variable-size sliding window): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Variable-size sliding window, tracking the count of the most frequent character as a proxy for replacement cost
Core Idea: A window's minimum replacement cost is its length minus its most frequent character's count; shrink whenever this cost exceeds the budget k
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Keeping the majority letter and replacing everything else is always the cheapest way to make a window uniform
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Track the majority letter's count; shrink only when replacing the rest would cost more than k
